text:
Hi! How are you? I am in Chicago with my family. We are at my aunt’s house. The house is near a big park, and we can walk there in five minutes.

Chicago is a big city, and the food is very good. We eat pizza and hot dogs. The pizza here is famous. My cousin says it is the best pizza in the city.

Tomorrow we are going to a baseball game. My father has four tickets. I am excited because I like baseball. My sister does not like baseball, but she likes the food at the stadium.

Do you like baseball? Write me later! Alex.

Barista: Good morning! What would you like?

Anna: A coffee, please. And a bagel.

Barista: The bagels are fresh today. We have plain, cheese, and sesame.

Anna: A cheese bagel, please.

Barista: Would you like milk in your coffee?

Anna: Yes, please. A little milk.

Barista: Anything else?

Anna: No, thank you. How much is it?

Barista: Five dollars. The coffee is hot, so be careful.

Anna: I will. I have a meeting at nine.

Barista: Good luck! Here is your order.

Anna: Here you are. Can I sit outside?

Barista: Yes, of course. The tables are near the door.

Anna: Thank you. Have a nice day!

Barista: You too! See you soon.

Dear Ben, I am in California for a week. The weather is warm and sunny. I am staying in a small hotel near the beach. My room has a balcony, and I can see the ocean from it.

In the morning I swim in the ocean, and in the afternoon I walk in the city. The streets are busy, but the people are friendly. Yesterday I visited a big market and bought a hat.

Today I saw a famous bridge. It was very long and red. I took many photos. The food here is great, but it is expensive. I am eating a lot of fruit.

See you soon! Max.

School starts on Monday, September 8. All students must be at school at 8:30. Please come to the main door, where a teacher will show you your classroom.

Please bring a notebook, two pens, and a water bottle. You do not need to bring books on the first day. The school will give you the books.

There is no class on Friday because it is a day off. The school library is open from 9:00 to 4:00 every day. You can borrow two books at a time.

On Tuesday, there is a short meeting for parents at 6:00 in the school hall. If you have questions, please call the school office.

We are happy to see you soon!

Hi, I am at the grocery store. We need milk, eggs, and bread for dinner. I am also buying apples and cheese. The apples are on sale, so I am buying two bags. The store is busy today, so I will be home at six.

Your father is at work, and your sister is at soccer practice. She will come home at five thirty.

Please clean your room before I come home. Put your books on the shelf and your clothes in the closet. Then you can watch TV for thirty minutes. Do not forget to feed the cat.

Dinner is at seven. We are having soup and bread. Love, Mom.

I live in a small city near the mountains. It is quiet, and the people are friendly. The city is not very big, so I can walk everywhere.

There is a big park in the center, and a river near my house. In the park, there is a playground and a small café. The café has the best ice cream in town.

In summer, my friends and I play soccer in the park. We also swim in the river when it is hot. In winter, we go skiing in the mountains. The ski school is cheap for students.

I like my city very much. It is a good place to live.

Hi Sam, I am happy because my cousin is visiting me next weekend. She lives in New York. I have not seen her for a year.

We are going to see a movie and eat pizza on Saturday. The movie starts at four, so we will meet at three thirty. We will take the bus at nine. On Sunday, we are going to the beach. My mother is going to make a picnic.

The weather is sunny, so we can swim. Can you come with us? My cousin is very funny, and she wants to meet you. Please write back and tell me if you are free.

See you soon! Leo.

My neighbor has a big brown dog. His name is Max. Max is three years old, and he is very friendly.

Every morning, Max runs in the yard and plays with a ball. He likes people, but he does not like cats. When he sees a cat, he barks loudly. My neighbor says, “Max, be quiet!” but Max does not listen.

In the evening, he sleeps near the door. My little sister loves Max and gives him food. Max is very careful with her. He sits and waits for her to give him a piece of bread.

Max is a good dog. He is part of the family.

Every summer, my family goes to the mountains. We stay in a small cabin for five days. The cabin is near a river, and there are many trees around it.

Every morning we walk in the forest. We see birds and sometimes deer. One day we saw a lake. The water was blue and very cold.

The water is cold, but my brother swims in it. My mother and I sit on the rocks and read. In the evening, we cook dinner and play cards. My father tells funny stories.

The trip is simple, but it is my favorite time of the year. I am already waiting for next summer.

Next week, our class has a project about animals. I am writing about dolphins. I chose dolphins because they are smart and interesting.

Dolphins are smart and friendly. They live in the ocean and eat fish. They can swim very fast. Some dolphins can jump high out of the water. They also talk to each other with sounds.

My friend Anna is drawing a picture of a dolphin. I am writing the text. We are presenting our project on Friday. We will show the picture and ask the class three questions.

I hope our project is good. I am a little nervous, but I am also excited.

Last month, a new family moved into the house next to Nora’s. The house was empty for a long time, so Nora was curious. She saw boxes, a bicycle, and a small dog in the yard. The family has two children, a boy and a girl. The boy is named Sam, and he is the same age as Nora.

On Saturday, Nora’s mother made a cake and asked Nora to take it to the new neighbors. Nora was nervous. She did not know what to say. She knocked on the door, and Sam opened it. “Hello,” Nora said. “My mother made this cake for you. Welcome to the neighborhood.” Sam smiled. “Thank you! Would you like to come in? My sister and I are making a puzzle.”

Nora went inside. The puzzle was a picture of a big city. Sam’s sister, Lily, showed Nora the pieces. They worked on the puzzle for an hour and drank lemonade. They talked about school, music, and their favorite books. Lily is two years younger, but she knew a lot about animals.

Now Nora and Sam walk to school together. They have become good friends. Nora is happy that she knocked on the door. She says, “Sometimes a small cake is the beginning of a big friendship.”

Last Friday, Class 8B went on a school trip to a science museum. They left school at eight o’clock and traveled by bus. The journey took one hour. On the bus, the students talked about the robots they wanted to see.

At the museum, a guide showed them a robot that could draw pictures. The students asked many questions. Then they visited a room about space. They saw a model of Mars and learned about the first moon landing. The guide explained how astronauts live and work in space.

After lunch, the class had a workshop. They built small cars from plastic pieces. The cars had to move using a balloon. Tom’s car went the fastest. Everyone clapped. The teacher took photos for the school website.

On the way home, the bus was quiet. Many students were tired, but they were happy. Their teacher said, “You asked excellent questions today. I am proud of you.” The next week, the class wrote a report about the trip. Tom wrote about the balloon cars. He said it was the best school trip of the year.

Leo used to drink two cans of soda every day. He also ate chips after school and did not exercise. He often felt tired, and he could not concentrate in class. His mother was worried, so she made an appointment with the doctor.

One day, his doctor said, “You do not need a special diet. You need three small habits.” First, Leo started drinking water instead of soda. Second, he walked to school instead of taking the bus. Third, he ate fruit for an afternoon snack. The doctor said, “Do not try to change everything at once.”

The first week was difficult. Leo missed the taste of soda, and he was hungry after school. But he did not give up. He wrote a note on his desk: “One small choice at a time.” His mother helped him by keeping a bottle of water in the fridge.

After a month, Leo felt better. He had more energy, and he could concentrate in class. He also slept better. His doctor was happy. Leo still drinks soda sometimes, but not every day. He says, “I did not change my whole life. I changed three small things.”

On Sunday afternoon, Maya and her friend Jess were shopping in the city center. Maya was trying on a jacket when she realized her phone was not in her bag. She looked in her pockets, under the chair, and on the floor. The phone was gone.

Maya was worried. Her phone had photos, messages, and her train ticket. Jess said, “Let’s go back to the last shop. Maybe someone found it.” They walked back to the bookstore. Maya asked the assistant, “Excuse me, did anyone find a phone?”

The assistant checked a drawer and smiled. “Is it a black phone with a blue case?” Maya said yes. A customer had found it near the magazines and given it to the assistant. The customer was still in the shop, so Maya thanked her too.

Maya was very happy. On the train home, she said to Jess, “I was lucky. Next time, I will keep my phone in my zipped pocket.” Jess laughed. “And I will check my bag before I try on a jacket.”

Three years ago, Ana started a small business from her kitchen. She made candles and sold them to friends and neighbors. At first, she had only ten customers. She worked in the evening, after her day job. Her kitchen smelled of lavender and lemon.

Ana learned quickly. She asked customers what they liked, and she changed her products. She started making candles with lavender and lemon. She also opened an online shop. Soon, people from other cities were buying her candles. Ana was surprised, but she was ready to work harder.

Last year, Ana moved her business into a small workshop. She hired one assistant, her cousin. They now sell about 300 candles a month. Ana still makes some candles herself, but she spends more time on planning and orders. She has also started using recycled boxes.

Ana says, “The most important thing was listening. I did not start with a perfect plan. I started with one product and learned from my customers.” She wants to open a second workshop next year, but she wants to grow slowly. “Fast growth is not always good growth,” she says.

Every summer, the town of Riverside has a festival in the park. Last year, the weather was sunny and dry. This year, the festival was different. In the morning, the sky was clear. Families arrived with blankets and food. Children played near the river.

At two o’clock, dark clouds appeared. The wind became stronger, and the first drops of rain fell. People ran to the school hall. The festival continued inside. The music group played, and the children made paper boats. Everyone was a little wet, but nobody was unhappy.

“We cannot change the weather,” said the mayor. “But we can change our plans.” The rain stopped at five o’clock. A rainbow appeared over the river. People went outside and took photos. The festival ended with a small fireworks show.

This year, the town will prepare two plans: one for sunny weather and one for rain. The mayor says, “If we are ready, the weather will not stop us.” The festival will also have a text-message alert so families know where to go.

Hi Mom and Dad, I am at camp, and I am fine. The camp is near a lake, and the water is cold but clean. I have already made three friends. Their names are Ben, Lily, and Sam. We sleep in a small cabin with four beds.

Every morning, we have breakfast at seven thirty. Then we have activities. Yesterday, I tried kayaking. It was difficult at first, but I did not fall in. In the afternoon, we hiked in the forest. We saw a deer and a lot of birds. My legs are tired, but I am happy.

The food is OK. We have pasta, soup, and fruit. I miss your cooking, Mom, but I am not hungry. Tomorrow, we are going to have a campfire. Ben is going to play the guitar, and Lily is going to tell a story. I am going to sing, but please do not laugh.

I will come home on Sunday afternoon. See you soon! Love, Alex.

Two years ago, an empty lot near the library was full of trash and dry grass. Nobody used it. Then a group of neighbors had an idea: why not turn it into a community garden? They asked the city for permission and promised to keep the area clean.

The city agreed to let them use the land for three years. The neighbors cleaned the lot and built twelve raised beds. They planted tomatoes, beans, herbs, and flowers. Some people did not have a garden, so they shared a bed with another family. Children helped to water the plants.

The garden has changed the neighborhood. People meet there on Saturdays and talk. Children learn where food comes from. The garden also helps the environment: the plants cool the air and the soil absorbs rainwater. The neighbors have started a small seed library, too.

The project is not perfect. Weeds grow quickly, and the water bill is higher than expected. But the neighbors have a plan. They will collect rainwater in two large barrels and ask local shops for help with tools. Maria, one of the organizers, says, “We did not wait for a big project. We started with one small garden. Now everyone knows their neighbors.”

Ava wanted to plan a surprise birthday party for her father. She asked her mother and brother for help. They decided to have the party on Saturday afternoon, when her father was at work. They had two weeks to prepare.

Ava made a list. She bought balloons, a cake, and fruit. Her brother cleaned the living room. Her mother called her father’s friends and invited them. They also made a photo album with old family pictures. Ava wrote a short speech for the party.

On Saturday, the family got ready. At three o’clock, the guests arrived. They hid in the living room and waited. When Ava’s father came home, everyone shouted, “Surprise!” He was very surprised. He laughed and said, “I thought I was coming home to a quiet afternoon!”

They ate cake and talked for hours. Ava’s father looked at the photo album and told stories about his childhood. He said it was the best birthday he could remember. After the party, Ava felt happy. She had worked hard, but the smile on her father’s face made everything worth it.

On the first day of school, a new student joined Class 8A. Her name was Rina, and she had moved from another city. She was quiet and sat alone at lunch. She did not know anyone, and she missed her old friends.

Two students, Omar and Lily, decided to talk to her. They asked where she was from and what she liked to do. Rina said she loved drawing and playing basketball. Omar said, “We have a basketball team. You should come to practice on Wednesday.”

On Wednesday, Rina went to practice. She was nervous, but the team was friendly. She was fast and good at passing. After practice, the coach said, “You can play with us this Saturday.” Rina started to feel better. She joined the art club too. She made a drawing of the school garden, and the art teacher put it on the wall.

By the end of the month, Rina had many friends. She still missed her old city sometimes, but she was happy. She said, “The first day was scary. Now I feel like I belong here.”

Every Saturday morning, a group of volunteers meets at the community center in the town of Riverton. They run a program called “Saturday Together.” The program offers free breakfast, homework help, and activities for children from low-income families.

The program started three years ago. At first, only five volunteers came. They used a small room and served simple food. Today, more than thirty volunteers help, and the program serves about eighty children every week. Local shops donate bread, fruit, and milk. A bakery gives day-old bread, and a grocery store gives fruit that is still good but cannot be sold.

The volunteers are not all teachers. Some are university students, some are retired people, and some are parents. They do different jobs. One group prepares food, another helps with homework, and another organizes games and art activities. A local doctor comes once a month to talk about health. A dentist visits twice a year.

The program has changed the lives of both children and volunteers. Children have a safe place to go on Saturday, and they get help with school. Volunteers learn new skills and meet people from different backgrounds. One volunteer, Mr. Davis, said, “I retired two years ago. I thought I would be bored. Now I have a reason to get up on Saturday.”

The program also has problems. The building is old, and the roof leaks when it rains. There is not enough space for all the children who want to come. The volunteers need more tables, books, and art supplies. They also need a second van to pick up children from distant neighborhoods. There is a waiting list of twenty children.

Last month, the town council promised to help. It will pay for a new roof and give the program a small grant. The volunteers are happy, but they know the money is not enough. They are planning a fundraising event in June. The event will include a concert, a food market, and a basketball game. Maria, the program coordinator, says, “We cannot solve every problem. But we can give children one good day each week. That is a start.”

Last year, the Jensen family decided to live without a car for twelve months. They wanted to reduce their carbon emissions and save money. They sold their old car and bought three bicycles and a cargo bike. The cargo bike was expensive, but it could carry two children and a week of shopping.

The first month was difficult. The father, Erik, used to drive to work. Now he cycles forty minutes each way. In winter, the ride is cold and dark. The mother, Anna, takes the children to school by cargo bike. On rainy days, they arrive wet. The children complained, and Erik sometimes wondered if the plan was realistic.

The family learned to plan. They shop once a week and carry food in the cargo bike. They use the bus for long trips and the train for visits to relatives. They also discovered that many places are closer than they thought. The bakery, the library, and the sports center are all within fifteen minutes by bike.

The children were not happy at first. They missed the car and the music they used to play. But they started to enjoy the ride. They noticed birds, trees, and neighbors they had never met. Their friends sometimes joined them on bikes. The family also saved money: they spent less on fuel, insurance, and repairs.

There were still challenges. When a child was sick, the family had to call a taxi. When they bought furniture, they needed a delivery service. And in winter, the cargo bike was sometimes too heavy. The family kept a small emergency fund for these situations.

At the end of the year, the family had a meeting. They decided not to buy another car. They kept the bicycles and the cargo bike. They also bought a small electric scooter for long trips. Erik says, “We are not perfect. We still use taxis sometimes. But we proved that a car is not always necessary. The first month was hard. After that, it became normal.”

Two years ago, the students at Westfield School started a newspaper. It began as a small project with eight students and one teacher. They wrote about school events, sports, and student achievements. The first issue was four pages long and printed in black and white.

Today, the newspaper has twenty students and a website. It publishes news, interviews, reviews, and opinion pieces. The team meets every Monday after school. They discuss ideas, assign stories, and edit drafts. The editor, Sam, checks the final version before it goes online.

The newspaper has had some important stories. Last year, it reported that the school cafeteria was throwing away too much food. The story included photos and numbers. After the article, the school started a food-sharing program. Another story explained how students could apply for scholarships. Several students said the article helped them.

The team has also made mistakes. Once, they published a story with the wrong date for a concert. Another time, they used a photo without permission. The teacher, Ms. Rivera, used these mistakes as lessons. She said, “A newspaper is powerful. If you make a mistake, correct it quickly and explain what happened.”

The team has rules. They check facts with two sources. They label opinion pieces clearly. They do not publish a student’s name without permission. They also allow anyone to reply to a story. These rules are not always easy to follow, but they protect the newspaper’s credibility.

Not everyone likes the newspaper. Some students say it is too serious. Others say it focuses on the same groups. The editors are trying to change this. They have started a section for new students and a comic strip. The newspaper has won a national award for student journalism, but the editors say the award is not the main goal. As Sam says, “We are not just writing stories. We are learning how to listen.”

When Daniel moved into his first apartment, he could not cook. He knew how to make toast and tea, but nothing else. He ate pasta with ready-made sauce and ordered pizza when he was tired. His kitchen had a stove, but he used it only to boil water.

One evening, his mother called. She asked, “What did you eat today?” Daniel laughed and said, “Pizza.” His mother was quiet for a moment. Then she said, “I will teach you three dishes. If you can cook three dishes, you can feed yourself.”

The first dish was tomato soup. Daniel followed his mother’s instructions by video. He cut the onions too quickly and cried. He added too much salt. The soup was not good, but he ate it. The second dish was chicken with rice. Daniel burned the chicken because he was watching his phone. He learned to stay near the stove. The third dish was a simple salad with eggs. This time, he did not burn anything. He was proud.

After a month, Daniel could cook the three dishes without help. He invited a friend for dinner. The friend said, “This is really good.” Daniel smiled. He had made the food himself. He still makes mistakes. Sometimes the rice is too hard, and sometimes the soup is too salty. But he is not afraid of the kitchen anymore. He has started to read recipes and watch cooking videos. He even bought a small notebook for his favorite dishes.

His mother visited him last month. He cooked dinner for her. She said, “You have learned more than cooking. You have learned to take care of yourself.” Daniel agreed. Cooking, he realized, is not only about food. It is about patience, attention, and the willingness to try again.

Some schools in the United States have started a four-day school week. Students go to school from Monday to Thursday, and Friday is free. The days are longer, usually by about an hour. Supporters say the schedule saves money and gives families more time together. Critics worry about childcare and learning.

One district in Colorado tried the schedule for three years. The district saved money on transport, heating, and substitute teachers. Attendance improved on the four school days. Teachers said they had more time for planning on Friday. Some students used Friday for sports, medical appointments, or extra help.

But the schedule also created problems. Many parents work on Friday and had to find childcare. Some students did not have a quiet place to study at home. Younger children missed the routine of a five-day week. The district offered Friday programs at two schools, but not all families could use them.

The results were mixed. Test scores did not change much. Some teachers said students were more tired because the days were longer. Others said the extra planning time improved their lessons. Parents were divided. One mother said, “I love having Friday with my children.” Another said, “I cannot afford another day of childcare.”

The district decided to keep the four-day week but to improve support. It opened a free Friday study center and asked local businesses to offer activities. It also surveyed families every year. The debate is not only about money. It is about what schools are for. If school is a place for learning, a four-day week may work if the learning is strong. If school is also a place for childcare and community, the schedule affects much more than the budget. As one teacher said, “A calendar is never just a calendar. It is a choice about how families live.”

When Mia adopted a dog from the shelter, she did not know what to expect. The dog, Bruno, was three years old and had lived on the street. He was afraid of loud noises and did not like strangers. The shelter said he needed a quiet home and patient owners.

The first weeks were difficult. Bruno hid under the table when visitors came. He barked at the door and pulled on the leash. Mia could not take him to the park without stress. She wondered if she had made a mistake. She called the shelter and asked for advice.

Mia asked a trainer for help. The trainer said, “Bruno is not a bad dog. He is scared. You need to teach him that the world is safe.” They started with small steps. Bruno learned to sit and wait. Mia gave him treats when he stayed calm. She walked him at quiet times and avoided crowded places.

After two months, Bruno began to change. He stopped hiding when the doorbell rang. He walked beside Mia instead of pulling. He even made a friend: a small dog named Coco. The two dogs played together in a fenced garden. Mia also learned to change. She became more patient and organized. She planned her day around Bruno’s walks and training. She read books about dog behavior and joined a local dog group.

One day, a neighbor’s child dropped a metal bowl. The noise was loud. Bruno looked scared, but he did not run. He stayed near Mia and waited. Mia gave him a treat and said, “Good boy.” She felt proud. Mia says, “Adopting Bruno was not easy. But he taught me that trust takes time. You cannot force it. You have to earn it.” Bruno is now a calm, friendly dog. He still does not like loud noises, but he has a home. And Mia has a friend.

Last year, Sofia joined a language exchange program at her school. The idea was simple: students who wanted to learn Spanish were paired with students who wanted to learn English. They met twice a week and spent half the time speaking each language. The program was free, and the school provided a room and coffee.

Sofia was nervous at first. She had studied Spanish for two years, but she had never spoken it with a native speaker. Her partner, Diego, was friendly and patient. He did not laugh at her mistakes. Instead, he helped her find the right words. On their first day, Sofia prepared ten questions, but she forgot them all. Diego said, “That is normal. Just talk about your day.”

At first, their conversations were short. They talked about school, families, and food. After a month, they could talk for an hour without stopping. Sofia learned useful expressions that were not in her textbook. Diego learned that English speakers often use short forms like “gonna” and “wanna”. They also discovered a funny false friend: “embarrassed” does not mean “pregnant”, although the Spanish word sounds similar.

The program changed Sofia’s attitude. She used to be afraid of making mistakes. Now she sees mistakes as part of learning. She says, “If you wait until you are perfect, you will never speak.” She also became more confident in class. Her teacher noticed that she raised her hand more often.

The exchange had one problem: time. Both students were busy, and sometimes they had to cancel. They solved this by meeting online when they could not meet in person. The program now has twenty pairs of students. In the spring, Diego’s family invited Sofia to dinner. She was nervous again, but she used what she had learned. She talked to Diego’s grandmother about cooking and learned three new recipes. She says that evening was the best test of her Spanish.

At the end of the year, Sofia and Diego gave a short presentation about their experience. They spoke in both languages, and the audience laughed at their stories. Sofia’s teacher says the exchange is valuable because it teaches real communication, not only grammar. Sofia agrees. She still makes mistakes, but she is no longer afraid to talk. She has also made a friend in another country.

When Mateo finished school, he had two offers. One was a place at a university to study engineering. The other was a job at a small company that built solar panels. The job paid a salary, and the university cost money. Mateo did not know what to choose. His family did not have much money, and he did not want to borrow a large loan.

His parents wanted him to go to university. They said a degree would give him more opportunities later. His uncle, who worked in construction, said the job was a chance to learn practical skills and earn money now. Mateo listened to both, but he felt confused. He liked working with his hands, but he also enjoyed reading and solving problems.

Mateo made a list of pros and cons. University offered theory, a network, and a qualification. The job offered experience, income, and training. He also thought about his learning style. He learned best when he could apply ideas to real problems. He visited both places. At the university, he liked the laboratories. At the company, he liked the team and the workshop.

In the end, Mateo chose a third option. He asked the company if he could work part-time and study part-time. The company agreed. It was not an easy schedule. On Mondays and Wednesdays, he attended classes. On Tuesdays and Thursdays, he worked. On Fridays, he studied and rested. He often felt tired, but he was learning quickly.

There were difficult weeks. Once, he had an exam on the same day as an important deadline. He talked to his manager and his teacher. Both gave him more time. He learned that asking early is better than pretending everything is fine. Two years later, Mateo is still studying and working. He has passed his first exams, and he has led a small project at the company.

He does not regret his decision. He says, “I did not want to choose between thinking and doing. I wanted both.” His advice to other students is simple: “Do not ask which option is better. Ask which option fits your life. And remember that you can sometimes create a third option.”

On the first Saturday of every month, a small café in the town of Hillford opens its doors for a different kind of event. People bring broken lamps, chairs, radios, and clothes. Volunteers help them repair the items for free. The café is called the Repair Café, and it has become a local tradition.

The Repair Café started two years ago. Its goal is to reduce waste and teach practical skills. Instead of throwing away a broken object, people learn how to fix it. The café has tools, sewing machines, and a team of volunteers with different skills. Local shops donate materials, and the town council gives a small grant.

One volunteer, Mr. Lee, is a retired electrician. He fixes lamps and small machines. Another volunteer, Ana, is a seamstress. She teaches people how to repair clothes. There is also a bicycle mechanic and a furniture maker. A young volunteer, Tom, is learning to sew. At first, he could not thread a needle. Now he can repair a jacket. He says, “I like making things last.”

The café is popular. On a busy day, it receives more than forty items. Some people come for the repair, but many come for the company. They drink coffee, talk, and share advice. The atmosphere is friendly and informal. One woman brought a chair that belonged to her grandmother. A volunteer repaired the leg, and she cried with happiness.

The café has limits. Some items are too broken to repair, and some repairs need expensive parts. The volunteers cannot fix everything. They also need more space and more young volunteers. But they believe the effort is worth it. The café also runs short workshops: Ana teaches people to mend socks, and Mr. Lee shows children how a simple circuit works. These workshops are free, and they are always full.

As Mr. Lee says, “A repair is a small act of respect. It says that this object still has value.”
